name: 泉仙 大慈院店 (Izusen Daijiin-ten)

claims.text: No gluten-free program is advertised; wheat-gluten (fu/namafu) and tempura are staple shojin ingredients, so cross-contact with wheat should be assumed.
Japanese soy sauce is standard in shojin seasoning and normally contains wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
This is an entirely plant-based shojin kitchen using no meat, fish or seafood, so animal cross-contact is inherently very low.

Fully vegetarian/vegan-leaning Buddhist cuisine where no meat, fish or seafood is prepared anywhere in the kitchen, and dashi is plant-based — a reassuring environment for vegans regarding animal cross-contact.
Long-established (since 1963) temple-grounds restaurant with a clear, published culinary philosophy.

name: 精進鉄鉢料理 泉仙 紫野店 (Izusen Murasakino (Shojin Teppachi Ryori)

claims.text: Wheat is integral to the cuisine — yuba, fu (wheat gluten) and standard soy sauce are used throughout — so a shared, wheat-heavy kitchen makes this unsuitable and unsafe for gluten-free or celiac diners.
Traditional Japanese soy sauce (wheat-containing) and other wheat-derived elements such as fu are described as essential to Izusen's cooking and cannot be modified.

As traditional shojin, the kitchen handles no meat and the menu is plant-based, which sharply reduces animal cross-contact — but it is not a certified vegan kitchen. A reviewer historically reported a bonito/fish flavour in the broth and said staff confirmed fish was once used for dashi; later reviewers reported no fish. Strict vegans should confirm no fish/katsuo dashi when booking.

Recent reviewers describe the service as very kind and attentive; however, an older account suggested staff were initially evasive about ingredient questions, so be clear and specific about dietary needs.

Fully plant-based shojin menu with no meat or seafood per the restaurant's own description — grains, legumes and vegetables only — making it broadly vegetarian/vegan-friendly with low animal cross-contact.
Long-praised, authentic shojin experience in a tranquil Daitoku-ji temple setting, well regarded by international visitors.

name: 泉仙 嵯峨野店 (Izusen Sagano)

claims.text: Wheat is structurally central to the cuisine (soy sauce and fu/wheat gluten are core ingredients; tempura uses wheat batter), so gluten is present throughout the kitchen and cross-contamination is effectively unavoidable for a GF diner.
Soy sauce used here is conventional wheat-containing soy sauce and is described as essential to Izusen's cooking and not modifiable.
The kitchen is a fully shojin (Buddhist vegetarian) operation serving no meat or fish, which greatly reduces the risk of animal cross-contact.
Entirely plant-based shojin ryori — no meat, no fish — so vegan and vegetarian diners can eat the standard set menus without modification.
Traditional shojin excludes the five pungent alliums (onion, garlic, etc.), helpful for diners avoiding those.

name: 鴨川ベーカリー 京都本店 (KAMOGAWA BAKERY Kyoto Honten (Kamogawa B)

claims.text: This is a wheat-flour bakery; all bread and bagels contain wheat and the kitchen is flour-heavy, so there is no gluten-free safe option and high airborne flour cross-contact.

Roughly 80% plant-based, but not a fully vegan shop: some bagel sandwiches contain salmon, shrimp and cream cheese, so animal products are handled in the same kitchen. Choose the plant-based loaves, bagels and plant-based burger and confirm fillings.
The shop was founded with allergy sufferers in mind, avoids butter, milk and eggs in its core breads, and offers an egg-allergy-friendly sandwich, indicating staff awareness of egg/dairy allergies.
Core breads use no butter, milk or eggs and rely on soy-milk butter and animal-free beet sugar, so plant-based options are clearly labeled and the menu is intentionally inclusive ('ONE TABLE').
No gluten-free program is documented; naan, papad and fried items share a kitchen with wheat, so a wheat-sensitive diner should ask before ordering.
This is an omnivore Indian kitchen that also serves meat and dairy dishes; many curries use cream or ghee, so vegan diners should request no dairy/eggs and confirm each dish.
English-speaking staff can tell which dishes can be made vegan and will confirm whether dips and accompaniments like chutneys are dairy/egg-free.
A wide range of vegetable-based and adaptable plant dishes (tofu/soybean curry, chana masala, aloo gobi, dal, vegetable pakoras, masala dosa), with staff used to advising vegan diners.
Vegetable-forward, Ayurveda-inspired menu makes plant-based ordering easier than at a typical non-vegetarian Indian restaurant.

name: 喫茶ホーボー堂 (Kissa Hobodo (Cafe Hobodo))

claims.text: No gluten-free protocol is documented; wheat-based items (homemade flatbread, gyoza/spring-roll wrappers, falafel, sweets) are prepared in the same small kitchen, so cross-contact with wheat should be assumed unless confirmed in person.
Set meals include miso soup and seasoned vegetable dishes; no source confirms wheat-free tamari is used, so standard wheat-containing soy sauce and miso should be assumed.
The entire kitchen is plant-based, so there is no risk of cross-contact with meat, fish, dairy, eggs or honey - every item served is vegan.
The owner-couple speak some English and provide an English menu, making it feasible to ask about ingredients; no formal allergen protocol is documented, so confirm specific needs directly with them.
100% vegan cafe and bookshop - all menu items are confirmed vegan, eliminating animal-product cross-contact concerns.
Produce is sourced from local organic and naturally-cultivated farms, and the menu is built around fresh seasonal vegetables.

name: 京大食堂 カフェテリアルネ (Kyodai Shokudo Cafeteria Rene)

claims.text: No allergen documentation was found; as a standard Japanese cafeteria, soy sauce and seasonings should be assumed to contain wheat unless staff confirm otherwise.

Certified-vegan dishes are prepared and served on a shared cafeteria line alongside meat and fish dishes, so incidental cross-contact is possible despite the vegan certification of the recipes themselves.
Plant-based dishes meet VegeProject Japan's vegan certification standard, meaning the recipes themselves contain no meat, fish, shellfish, dairy, eggs, or honey.
Vegan and halal items are clearly labeled and the venue is open to the public, making it an easy, low-cost option for plant-based diners visiting the campus area.

name: 京大食堂 北部食堂 (Kyodai Shokudo Hokubu Shokudo (Kyoto Uni)

claims.text: High-volume cafeteria serving fried foods and wheat noodles alongside vegan dishes; wheat cross-contact is likely and no gluten-free protocol is documented.
No wheat-free soy sauce is confirmed; standard Japanese soy sauce and cafeteria seasonings typically contain wheat, so assume soy sauce is not gluten-free unless verified with staff.

Vegan dishes are prepared and served in a shared omnivore cafeteria line; the vegan menu itself is certified to contain no animal-derived ingredients, but cross-contact in a shared kitchen is possible.
Menu cards display nutritional balance and allergen information; staff recommend telling them about vegetarian/vegan needs and any allergies before choosing a dish.
Carries a VegeProject-certified vegan menu defined as containing no meat, seafood, eggs, dairy or honey, with items clearly labeled.
Open to the public (not only students), making the certified vegan options accessible to travelers.
